sections.title: The Gateway: How can one hook and one string make lace, toys and blankets?
sections.html:
Web address: /crochet/one-hook-one-string/ · Keywords: crochet for beginners, what is crochet, crochet history, crochet stitches, crochet vs knitting

Crochet needs almost nothing: a hook and a length of yarn or thread. Yet with them people make fine lace collars, stuffed toys, warm blankets, bags, rugs, even sculptures. Every crochet piece is built one loop at a time, pulled through another loop, and only one loop is "live" on the hook at any moment. That simple rule is crochet's freedom: you can go in any direction, in rows, in rounds or in free shapes.

This short course asks one question in five steps: what makes crochet special, and why do people love it?

By the end you will be able to:

  • Say what crochet is and how it differs from knitting.
  • Explain why no machine truly crochets.
  • Give the main theories of where crochet came from.
  • Tell the story of Irish crochet lace and the Great Famine.
  • Explain, with evidence, why many people find crochet calming.

sections.title: What is crochet, really?
sections.html:
Short answer: Crochet is making fabric from a continuous strand by pulling loops through other loops with a hooked tool. The word comes from the French crochet, "small hook". Unlike knitting, which keeps a whole row of live loops on needles, crochet works one stitch at a time and finishes each before moving on.

Keywords: what is crochet, crochet meaning, crochet vs knitting, crochet vs tatting, crochet hook

How it compares

  • Knitting (KNT): many live loops on two or more needles; stretchy, thinner fabric.
  • Crochet: one live loop; thicker, firmer fabric; easy to shape in three dimensions.
  • Tatting: lace made of knots and rings with a shuttle or needle.
  • Knotting and macramé: fabric from knots, no hook needed.
  • Nalbinding: an older looping craft with a single eye-needle and short lengths.

Why it is flexible

Because each stitch is finished, a dropped hook does not unravel a whole row, and you can add stitches anywhere. That is why crochet suits round shapes (granny squares, toys) and freeform art.

Remember this: One hook, one live loop, endless shapes.

sections.title: Why can't a machine crochet the way it knits?
sections.html:
Short answer: Each crochet stitch involves the hook moving in several directions, wrapping yarn and passing through loops at different heights and angles. Machines handle the regular, repeated motion of knitting needles well, but no machine has yet copied true hand crochet. Factory "crochet-look" lace is usually made on warp-knitting or other machines.

Keywords: crochet machine, is crochet handmade, machine knitting vs crochet, crochet look lace

What this means

  • Every crocheted item is handmade. A crocheted cardigan or toy in a shop was made by a person, often a low-paid worker; ask who made it (CRO-17).
  • Imitations: "crochet" lace trims are often made on machines that imitate the look.
  • Value: hand crochet takes hours; a blanket can take 40 hours or more.

Remember this: If it is truly crocheted, a human made it.

Next: Who made it first? Where did crochet come from?

sections.title: Where did crochet come from?
sections.html:
Short answer: Nobody knows for sure. Looping crafts are ancient, but clear evidence of crochet as we know it appears only in the early 1800s in Europe. The first published crochet patterns are usually traced to the Dutch magazine Penélopé in 1824. Earlier theories point to Arabia, South America or China, but evidence is thin.

Keywords: history of crochet, origin of crochet, Penelope 1824, shepherd's knitting, tambour embroidery

The theories

  • Arabian origin, spreading along trade routes (Lis Paludan, Crochet: History and Technique, 1995, found no firm proof).
  • South American puberty-rite adornments, mentioned in some histories.
  • Chinese three-dimensional dolls.
  • Tambour embroidery: a hook used to chain-stitch on fabric stretched on a frame, popular in India, Persia and Turkey; some historians think crochet began when people dropped the fabric and worked the chain "in the air" (crochet in the air).
  • "Shepherd's knitting": slip-stitch crochet in 19th-century Scotland.

What is certain

By the 1840s, crochet pattern books were popular in Europe, and Mlle Riego de la Branchardière published many designs that made crochet lace fashionable.

Remember this: Crochet is younger than knitting in the records, and its birthplace is still a mystery.

Next: In Ireland, crochet was a lifeline. How?

sections.title: How did crochet save families in the Irish famine?
sections.html:
Short answer: During the Great Famine of 1845 to 1852, nuns and charitable women taught girls and women to make crochet lace imitating costly Venetian needle lace. Sold in Britain, Europe and America, it brought cash to families who had lost their potato crop. "Irish crochet" became world-famous.

Keywords: Irish crochet lace, Great Famine crochet, Clones lace, crochet history Ireland, crochet cottage industry

How it worked

  • Teaching: the Ursuline nuns at Blackrock, Cork, and others ran classes from the 1840s.
  • Motifs: roses, shamrocks and leaves were made separately and joined with a mesh of chains.
  • Centres: Clones (County Monaghan) gave its name to "Clones lace".
  • Income: families sometimes earned more from lace than from farm work; some lace-makers saved enough to emigrate.

Echoes in India

The same story repeats: in 1844, Scottish missionaries are said to have taught crochet in Narsapur, Andhra Pradesh, and it became a livelihood for tens of thousands of women. Narsapur crochet lace now has a GI tag (CRO-07).

Remember this: Crochet lace turned skill into survival.

sections.title: Why is crocheting calming?
sections.html:
Short answer: Repetitive, rhythmic hand movements, a clear goal and a finished object seem to calm the mind. In a 2020 online survey of over 8,000 crocheters, Pippa Burns and Rosemary Van Der Meer found that about 90 per cent said crochet made them calmer, and many used it to cope with anxiety, grief or chronic pain.

Keywords: crochet and mental health, crochet mindfulness, benefits of crochet, crafting and anxiety, textile crafts well-being

What studies say

  • Burns and Van Der Meer (Perspectives in Public Health, 2021): crochet linked with feeling calmer, happier and more useful.
  • Riley, Corkhill and Morris (2013) on knitting: similar calm and social benefits (KNT-14).
  • Flow: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's idea of absorption in a task that matches your skill.
  • Social crafting: groups and "crochet-alongs" reduce loneliness.

Honest limits

These are surveys of people who already crochet; they show association, not proof. Crochet complements, never replaces, professional care.

Remember this: Rhythm, purpose and community make crochet a calming craft.

sections.title: Hooks
sections.html:
Before you start — CRO-02. Hook sizes are best given in millimetres, the international standard. The US uses letters and numbers (for example US H-8 = 5 mm); old UK sizes ran backwards (UK 6 = 5 mm). Steel hooks for thread use their own small numbers. Always check the millimetre size.
  • CRO-02.1 Standard hooks: aluminium (smooth, cheap), steel (0.5 to 2.75 mm, for thread and lace), wood and bamboo (warm, less slippery), plastic (large sizes).
  • CRO-02.2 Ergonomic hooks: thick, soft handles to reduce hand strain.
  • CRO-02.3 Inline and tapered heads: inline heads (Bates style) suit some people, tapered (Boye style) suit others.
  • CRO-02.4 Tunisian (afghan) hooks: long hooks, often with a cable, to hold many loops (CRO-04.6).
  • CRO-02.5 Double-ended hooks: for two-colour reversible Tunisian work ("crochet on the double").
  • CRO-02.6 Jumbo hooks: 15 to 25 mm and more, for chunky and arm-style work.
  • CRO-02.7 Light-up and specialty hooks: hooks with lights for dark yarn; hairpin forks and broomstick pins (CRO-07).
sections.summary: -  CRO-02.1 Standard hooks: aluminium (smooth, cheap), steel (0.5 to 2.75 mm, for thread and lace), wood and bamboo (warm, less slippery), plastic (large sizes).

sections.title: Yarns, fibres and notions
sections.html:
• CRO-03.1 Yarn weights (Craft Yarn Council system): 0 lace, 1 super fine (fingering), 2 fine (sport), 3 light (DK), 4 medium (worsted, aran), 5 bulky, 6 super bulky, 7 jumbo; the UK uses "ply" names; the label lists suggested hook size and gauge.
  • CRO-03.2 Cotton: firm, washable, good for amigurumi, dishcloths and summer tops; mercerised cotton thread for lace.
  • CRO-03.3 Wool: warm, springy, can felt; merino is soft; superwash wool survives machines.
  • CRO-03.4 Acrylic: cheap, washable, many colours; does not breathe and sheds microplastics (CRO-15.3).
  • CRO-03.5 Blends and other fibres: bamboo viscose, linen, silk, alpaca, mohair; India's own jute, banana-fibre and khadi yarns.
  • CRO-03.6 Recycled yarns: t-shirt yarn ("tarn"), plarn (plastic bag yarn), sari-silk yarn from Indian waste silk.
  • CRO-03.7 Notions: stitch markers, tapestry needles, scissors, tape measure, row counter, safety eyes for toys, stuffing, blocking mats and pins, buttons.

parts.intro: About this Part. Every stitch with one or two lines. US and UK names differ for the same stitch: a US "single crochet" is a UK "double crochet". Patterns state which system they use; this booklet uses US names with UK names in brackets.

sections.title: Textured, post, colourwork and lace stitches
sections.html:
• CRO-05.1 Bobble: several unfinished double crochets in one stitch, closed together; makes a raised dot.
  • CRO-05.2 Puff: several loops pulled up in one stitch; soft, rounded.
  • CRO-05.3 Popcorn: several complete stitches folded and closed; pops to the front.
  • CRO-05.4 Cluster: stitches worked into several stitches and joined at the top.
  • CRO-05.5 Shell and fan: several stitches in one place, fanning out; the base of many lace edgings.
  • CRO-05.6 V-stitch: a double, chain, double in one stitch.
  • CRO-05.7 Bullion: yarn wrapped many times round the hook; a coil, used in Irish lace.
  • CRO-05.8 Crocodile stitch: overlapping scales.
  • CRO-05.9 Post stitches: worked around the stem of a stitch from the front or back; make cables and crochet ribbing.
  • CRO-05.10 Tapestry crochet: carrying unused colours inside stitches; famous in Colombia's Wayuu mochila bags and Guatemala.
  • CRO-05.11 Mosaic crochet: patterns from stitches dropped down over earlier rows; one colour per row.
  • CRO-05.12 Intarsia: separate yarn for each colour block; large pictures with no carried strands.
  • CRO-05.13 Lace stitches: mesh, picot, pineapple, spider, Solomon's knot (love knot).
  • CRO-05.14 Tunisian stitches: simple stitch, knit stitch (looks like knitting), purl stitch, full stitch, honeycomb; worked forward and back on a long hook.
  • CRO-05.15 Surface crochet: chain stitches on top of finished fabric, like embroidery.
sections.summary: -  CRO-05.1 Bobble: several unfinished double crochets in one stitch, closed together; makes a raised dot.

sections.title: Making and finishing
sections.html:
• CRO-06.1 Rows versus rounds: rows turn at the end; rounds spiral or join; rounds suit hats, toys and squares.
  • CRO-06.2 Magic ring (adjustable ring): a loop pulled tight to close the centre of a round.
  • CRO-06.3 Increasing and decreasing: two stitches in one to grow; two stitches worked together to shrink (invisible decrease for toys).
  • CRO-06.4 Turning chains: the extra chains at a row's start that match the stitch height.
  • CRO-06.5 Changing colours: finishing the last stitch in the new colour.
  • CRO-06.6 Joining: slip-stitch, single crochet, whip stitch, join-as-you-go for squares.
  • CRO-06.7 Weaving in ends: through stitches in several directions so they do not slip out.
  • CRO-06.8 Blocking: wetting or steaming and pinning work to shape; essential for lace (not for acrylic with heat).
  • CRO-06.9 Gauge (tension): stitches and rows per 10 cm; make a swatch so garments fit.
  • CRO-06.10 Reading patterns: abbreviations, brackets and repeats, asterisks, stitch counts.
  • CRO-06.11 Reading charts: international symbols (as in Japanese pattern books), read from the centre out for rounds.
  • CRO-06.12 Left-handed crochet: mirror the instructions; charts are reversed.
  • CRO-06.13 Edgings and borders: crab stitch (reverse single crochet), picot edging, shell borders.
sections.summary: -  CRO-06.1 Rows versus rounds: rows turn at the end; rounds spiral or join; rounds suit hats, toys and squares.

sections.title: Styles and traditions of the world and India
sections.html:
• CRO-07.1 Irish crochet lace: separately made motifs joined with mesh (CRO-00.04).
  • CRO-07.2 Filet crochet: a grid of filled and open squares that makes pictures; easy to chart.
  • CRO-07.3 Tunisian (afghan) crochet: a dense, woven-looking fabric on a long hook.
  • CRO-07.4 Broomstick lace: loops pulled up onto a thick pin (once a broom handle) and worked off in groups.
  • CRO-07.5 Hairpin lace: strips worked on a U-shaped fork and joined; Victorian favourite.
  • CRO-07.6 Amigurumi: Japanese crocheted (or knitted) stuffed toys, worked in tight spirals; ami means knitted or crocheted, nuigurumi means stuffed doll.
  • CRO-07.7 Freeform crochet: improvised shapes and textures; Prudence Mapstone and James Walters and Sylvia Cosh pioneered it.
  • CRO-07.8 Overlay and Bavarian crochet: overlay builds raised patterns on a base; Bavarian is a dense, two-sided round technique.
  • CRO-07.9 Tapestry and Wayuu mochila bags: the Wayuu women of La Guajira, Colombia and Venezuela; each design carries meaning.
  • CRO-07.10 Granny squares: motifs worked in rounds and joined; 1970s icons, back in fashion in the 2020s.
  • CRO-07.11 Crochet art and yarn bombing: the Crochet Coral Reef (Margaret and Christine Wertheim, from 2005), which links crochet and hyperbolic geometry (Daina Taimiņa's crocheted hyperbolic planes, 1997); guerrilla "yarn bombing" of public objects.
  • CRO-07.12 India: Narsapur crochet lace: Andhra Pradesh's West Godavari region; tablecloths, bedspreads and doilies in fine cotton thread; GI tag (registered 2003 to 2004); a women's home industry, mostly exported.
  • CRO-07.13 India: Goa and Kerala: Portuguese-era lace and crochet traditions in Goan Catholic homes; convent schools in Kerala and Goa that taught crochet; church linens and christening robes.
  • CRO-07.14 India: everyday crochet: crosia (Hindi word) work in North Indian homes: doilies, TV covers, toran door hangings, purses, baby sweaters; often taught by mothers and grandmothers.
  • CRO-07.15 Other traditions: Turkish oya lace edgings (needle, hook and shuttle forms), Philippine and Latin American crochet, Russian and Ukrainian crochet lace.
sections.summary: -  CRO-07.1 Irish crochet lace: separately made motifs joined with mesh (CRO-00.04).

sections.title: Designers, artists and community
sections.html:
• CRO-10.1 Historic figures: Mlle Riego de la Branchardière (pattern author, 1840s to 1880s); the Ursuline nuns of Blackrock; Queen Victoria, who crocheted scarves for soldiers in the Boer War (by tradition).
  • CRO-10.2 Designers and teachers: Lily Chin, Jean Leinhauser, Doris Chan, Annie Modesitt, Robyn Chachula, Dora Ohrenstein, Edie Eckman (stitch dictionaries), Jonathan Hiller, Lucy of Attic24 (colourful blogs), Tamara Kelly (Moogly).
  • CRO-10.3 Artists: Joana Vasconcelos (crochet-covered sculptures), Olek (Agata Oleksiak), Toshiko Horiuchi MacAdam (giant crocheted and knitted playgrounds), the Wertheim sisters (Crochet Coral Reef), Daina Taimiņa (hyperbolic crochet).
  • CRO-10.4 Indian makers: the women lace-makers of Narsapur and their cooperatives; self-help groups across India; Indian crochet designers and teachers online (choose those who credit patterns).
  • CRO-10.5 Guilds and communities: Crochet Guild of America (1994), Crochet Guild of Great Britain (1995), Ravelry (2007), local crochet circles, crochet-alongs (CALs).
  • CRO-10.6 Fairs and competitions: CGOA design competitions, county and state fair crochet categories, India's handicraft fairs (Dilli Haat, Surajkund International Crafts Mela).
  • CRO-10.7 Records and big projects: community blankets and record attempts listed by Guinness World Records; check guinnessworldrecords.com for current holders.

sections.html:

  • CRO-12.2 Crochet as livelihood: Irish famine lace, Narsapur, Wayuu bags; fair pay for makers.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.html:
• CRO-14.1 Edges not straight: count stitches; check the turning chain and last stitch.
  • CRO-14.2 Work too tight or loose: change hook size, relax the hand, check gauge.
  • CRO-14.3 Squares curling or rippling: too few or too many stitches per round.
  • CRO-14.4 Holes in amigurumi: smaller hook, invisible decrease, tighter tension.
  • CRO-14.5 Hand pain: ergonomic hook, breaks, stretches; see a doctor for persistent pain.
sections.summary: -  CRO-14.1 Edges not straight: count stitches; check the turning chain and last stitch.

sections.title: Care and selling
sections.html:
• CRO-15.1 Care: follow the yarn label; hand-wash wool in cool water; dry flat; never hang heavy pieces.
  • CRO-15.2 Storage: clean, dry, with neem leaves or cedar against moths.
  • CRO-15.3 Selling handmade ethically: price for time and materials; credit and respect pattern licences (many designers allow selling finished items, some do not); honest fibre labels; safety standards for children's toys (secure eyes, no small parts for under-3s).
sections.summary: -  CRO-15.1 Care: follow the yarn label; hand-wash wool in cool water; dry flat; never hang heavy pieces.

sections.title: Editor's notes (corrections and decisions on the brief)
sections.html:
1. US and UK stitch names are both given, because they cause most beginner confusion.
  2. Crochet's origins are presented as unknown, with the main theories and the 1824 first printed patterns.
  3. "Crochet machines" are corrected: true crochet is handmade.
  4. The Narsapur 1844 story is marked as local account; the GI tag is official.
  5. Records are pointed to Guinness World Records rather than stated, since they change.
  6. Added beyond the brief: hyperbolic crochet and maths, yarn bombing, toy-safety rules, pattern licences, and acrylic microplastics.
